newsitem.title: UK: Dollar spikes up in Europe as market heads into G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar spikes up in Europe as market heads into G7.

text.p: Dollar sentiment was buoyant at the end of the week in Europe, with its break above the 1.72-marks level triggering stop-loss buying and a further rise which pulled dollar/yen up with it.

Traders said the dollar had been nudged down a bit too far for comfort against the yen and mark this week despite its underlying strength, and that position adjustment was going ahead before the G7 finance ministers' meeting this weekend.
"The dollar was looking a bit oversold and we'd taken out a very short-term downtrend," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives trading at the Cooperative Bank in London.
"Now that we've broken out of that trend, we're heading towards the 1.7250-marks area," Beauchamp said.
The dollar was at 1.7225/32 marks at 1535 GMT, just off the day's high, and up from 1.7153/58 in late European trade on Thursday. It was at 125.90/95 yen against 125.87/97 on Thursday.
Some traders said dollar/mark may have been helped by the dollar's strength against other European currencies today.

The mark had gained on its European crosses on renewed worries over European monetary union and next month's French elections, and this had led to selling of European currencies against the dollar as well, they said.

"When there's nervousness over EMU the market tends to sell European currencies for marks. But it seems they're selling them against the dollar as well today, since they want both dollars and marks ahead of the G7," said one trader at a U.S. bank here.
The dollar was at 5.8150/80 French francs against Thursday's 5.7874/84. Against the lira, a currency vulnerable to jitters over EMU, it was at 1715.80/6.80 against 1705.61/6.11.

Mark/Paris had been strong today on an opinion poll showing France's ruling coalition was expected to win the election by only a tiny majority, since there were fears that a win by the opposition would shackle France's efforts to join EMU.

But traders were loath to push the dollar too far in either direction, particularly against the yen, ahead of the G7 meeting and summit talks between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto scheduled for today.
Clinton is due to hold a news conference at 1830 GMT, while his Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will hold a pre-G7 briefing at 1700 GMT.

Dollar/yen will only try to recoup the losses it made earlier, traders said. Overnight, dollar/yen was dampened by a rise in Japanese market interest rates stemming from the failure of Japanese life insurer Nissan Mutual Life Insurance.

Nissan said it had been hit by Japan's record-low interest rates which slashed returns on its investments, and analysts said this highlighted the dilemma in Japan's monetary policy, which had been kept easy to help the nation's fragile economy.
"With this business suspension, the market began to nurture a perception that Japan's interest rates might go up," said Toshiyuki Suzuki, market economist at Sanwa Bank in London.

"This is because Japanese government bond prices dropped on fears that in this situation, Nissan might have to sell off some financial assets. And also because of the view that Japan's low interest rates had been a hindrance to the company," he said.
Meanwhile, analysts said the G7 meeting was unlikely to yield a strongly worded statement on currencies, and that any comment would likely target dollar/yen rather than dollar/mark.

"It's clear the German authorities have no interest in influencing dollar/mark, and they're happy with it where it is. So we aren't expecting the G7 to do anything about it," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank. "If the G7 turns out as we expect, which would be basically in line with the Berlin G7 meeting, the dollar should pick up after the meeting."
